case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Caucasian woman, a non-smoker with no relevant drug history, presented during routine follow-up for bullous pemphigoid (in remission) with progressive, asymptomatic blackish pigmentation of both buccal mucosa. She also reported a 7-year history of brownish-black pigmentation of several fingernails. No family members were affected. 

On examination, there was a regular, brownish, reticular pattern on both sides of the buccal mucosa. Multiple longitudinal pigmented bands were present on her fingernails and toenails. Potassium hydroxide preparation and fungal cultures were negative. Digital dermoscopy of the nails showed a pseudo-Hutchinson’s sign, with homogeneous brownish and grayish longitudinal bands and lines with ill-defined margins on the nail plate.

Laboratory tests—including erythrocyte sedimentation rate; complete blood count with differential; urinalysis; lipid profile; renal and liver function tests; serum amylase, lipase, and lactate dehydrogenase; tumor markers (CEA, AFP, CA 19-9); and immunology parameters (antinuclear antibodies, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins)—were all within normal limits. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities. Colonoscopy revealed no tumorous formations. Endocrinologic evaluation, including cortisol levels, antipituitary antibodies, and an ACTH stimulation test, was normal. The patient declined biopsy of the oral lesions.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Nail melanoma — “Dermoscopy is a useful, non-invasive, diagnostic procedure that allows us to differentiate LHS pigmented lesions from nail melanoma.” 2. Medication-induced melanonychia — “Medication-induced melanonychia ... may have similar dermoscopic patterns.” 3. Ethnic-type melanonychia — “Medication-induced melanonychia or ethnic-type melanonychia may have similar dermoscopic patterns.” 4. Drug-induced mucosal pigmentation — “Drug-induced pigmentation usually occurs after months or years of chronic drug use, and tends to resolve once drugs are discontinued.” 5. Smoker’s melanosis — “Smoking can result in oral, mucosal pigmentation called smoker's melanosis ... and it is not associated with pigmentation of the nails.” 6. Physiologic (racial) pigmentation — “Physiologic (racial) pigmentation of the oral mucosa appears in Asians, Blacks, and other dark-skinned persons, resembling LHS.” 7. Addison’s disease — “Patients with Addison's disease also have low blood pressure, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and elevated blood urea nitrogen, due to their adrenocortical insufficiency.” 8. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome — “PJS is an autosomal dominant inherited condition featuring a combination of mucocutaneous pigmentation, intestinal polyposis and, importantly, predisposition to various types of cancer.” 9. Bandler syndrome — “BS lesions present at birth ... characterized by intestinal, vascular malformation that can cause significant gastrointestinal bleeding.” 10. McCune-Albright syndrome — “MCAS includes labial and genital pigmentation but is often unilateral and does not involve the nails. The disease is also accompanied by precocious puberty in females and fibrous dysplasia.”

selection.screen_reason: Acquired buccal macular pigmentation with longitudinal melanonychia, no family history and a negative systemic workup give Laugier-Hunziker syndrome.
selection.second_look_note: Acquired adult-onset oral and nail pigmentation with no drugs, smoking or affected relatives is history that excludes key mimics; exam and a negative systemic workup decide.
